title: Ready for the real world?
objective: Six quick questions. One starting point. A simple way forward.
intro: Think about one goal and use what you learned about time, access and risk. You can use your own situation or a fictional example.
disclaimer: An educational starting point, not personal financial advice or a product recommendation. Investments can lose value; you do not have to open an account or buy anything.
longTermReason: You have a long, flexible horizon, spare money and room to handle market swings.

questions.label: What is your age group?
questions.help: Age adds context, not an automatic risk level.

questions.label: What are you saving for?
questions.help: Choose just one goal for this plan.

questions.label: When will you first need the money?
questions.help: Use the earliest likely withdrawal date.

questions.label: Are your financial basics covered?
questions.help: An emergency buffer is separate, accessible money for essential expenses.

options.label: Yes: 3+ months saved, no expensive debt, money is spare
I still need an emergency buffer

questions.label: Could you wait if markets fell?
questions.help: Think about what you can afford, not just how a loss feels.

options.label: Yes, I could wait several extra years

I may need the money early

questions.label: How would a 20% fall feel?
questions.help: Imagine 1,000 becoming 800. Losses can be larger and recovery is not guaranteed.

options.label: Too stressful — I would want to sell

when.reason: Check account eligibility with a parent or guardian before any real-money step.
A separate emergency buffer helps you avoid selling investments to cover surprises.
Essential bills and expensive debt come before exposing spare money to market risk.
Define the goal before choosing an investment.
Your first withdrawal date helps determine how much risk the money can withstand.
Check your buffer, debt and essential spending before deciding what is spare.
Work out whether an early withdrawal or a loss would disrupt the goal.
More practice can help you explore a level of fluctuation you could live with.
Emergency money needs ready access, not stock-market risk.
You may need the money within three years, leaving little time to withstand a market fall.
Access and protecting the required amount matter more than chasing growth for this goal.
Smaller fluctuations are more consistent with the comfort level you described.

guardian.title: Start with a parent or guardian
guardian.summary: Explore eligible youth savings together and keep practising with virtual money.
guardian.tradeoff: Age limits, ownership and withdrawal rules vary by country.

steps.title: Share your goal
steps.body: Talk to a parent or guardian.

steps.title: Compare youth accounts
steps.body: Use regulated banks' official websites.

steps.title: Check the rules
steps.body: Ask a bank about eligibility and consent.

steps.title: Decide together
steps.body: Keep learning; no purchase is required.

foundations.title: Build a buffer before investing
foundations.summary: An easy-access savings account is a useful starting point while you build emergency savings and address expensive debt.
foundations.tradeoff: Savings may trail inflation, but having accessible money can prevent forced selling.

steps.title: Check bills and debt
steps.body: Cover essentials; review expensive debt.

steps.title: Compare savings accounts
steps.body: Look at regulated banks' official sites.

steps.title: Check access and fees
steps.body: Verify withdrawal terms and deposit protection.

steps.title: Build your buffer
steps.body: Save affordably, then revisit investing.

clarify.title: Make the goal clearer first
clarify.summary: A short planning conversation is a better next step than choosing stocks or a fund while key answers are uncertain.
clarify.tradeoff: Waiting is an option. You do not need to guess or buy something to complete the lesson.

steps.title: Name the goal
steps.body: Write down the amount and first withdrawal date.

steps.title: Check your budget
steps.body: Identify your buffer, debt and spare money.

steps.title: Ask for help
steps.body: Contact a qualified, regulated adviser if needed.

steps.title: Try again
steps.body: Update these six answers when ready.

accessible.title: Start by comparing savings accounts
accessible.summary: For this goal, easy-access savings fit better than stocks or stock ETFs. Consider a term deposit only for money you will not need before maturity.
accessible.tradeoff: Returns may not beat inflation. Fixed-term deposits can restrict access or charge an early-exit penalty.

steps.title: Compare 2–3 banks
steps.body: Use their official savings pages.

steps.title: Check the small print
steps.body: Verify regulation, fees, access and deposit protection.

steps.title: Open if it fits
steps.body: Use the verified bank app, website or branch.

steps.title: Build a saving habit
steps.body: Set an affordable transfer and review the rate.

cautious.title: Compare deposits and high-quality bonds
cautious.summary: Start with savings or deposits that match your deadline. Learn about high-quality bonds before considering market-risk money for this goal.
cautious.tradeoff: Bonds can lose value or default; bond funds do not promise your original money back on a set date.

steps.title: Set the goal date
steps.body: Keep money needed soon accessible.

steps.title: Compare options
steps.body: Read official bank and bond information.

steps.title: Speak to an adviser
steps.body: Ask about fees, losses, access and commissions.

steps.title: Choose when ready
steps.body: Verify the provider and terms before opening an account.

diversified.title: Explore a broad-market index fund or ETF
diversified.summary: A low-cost, diversified, unleveraged fund is a reasonable category to study for this long-term goal, with emergency savings kept separate.
diversified.tradeoff: Large losses are possible, even over long periods. A narrow or leveraged ETF is not the same as a broad-market fund.

steps.title: Compare providers
steps.body: Research regulated banks, brokers or fund platforms.

steps.title: Check risks and fees
steps.body: Verify the licence, holdings, all costs and local tax rules.

steps.title: Open an account
steps.body: If you choose, use a verified channel for identity checks.

steps.title: Start small, review yearly
steps.body: Only invest spare money once you understand the product.

contextNotes.text: For retirement, also compare employer and personal pension accounts: check fees, tax rules and withdrawal lock-ups.
As withdrawals approach, review how a market fall would affect them. Age alone does not determine your investment mix.

providerCheck: Before opening an account, check the provider's legal entity, permissions and warning lists with your local regulator. A licence is not an endorsement or protection against market losses. Ask an adviser how they are paid.
